rows.label: Ineffective goods
rows.explainer: Purchased LLINs will be WHO pre-qualified. The difference in effectiveness of brands is incorporated into the adjustment for effective coverage years.

rows.label: Goods purchased and left in storage until they expire / Cash doesn't reach recipients or is taken back from them inappropriately
rows.explainer: Our cost per net analysis does not adjust for nets that are purchased and do not reach households, so we adjust for that here. Malaria Consortium expects to purchase 10% more LLINs than the estimated need. If extra LLINs remain at the end of the campaign, it is expected that they will be given to clinics to hand out as part of "continuous distribution" to vulnerable groups, such as pregnant women and young children. This value assumes that some, but not all, of the buffer stock will achieve a similar impact as LLINs distributed during the campaign.

Misappropriation without monitoring results
rows.explainer: Malaria Consortium will conduct, at a minimum, coverage surveys following campaigns in these states. It may conduct other monitoring in addition.

rows.label: False monitoring results
rows.explainer: We have conducted a relatively thorough review of Malaria Consortium's coverage surveys for SMC from recent years; we thus believe we have identified most major risks of bias. We have limited visibility into the quality of survey implementation due to data collectors' involvement in respondent selection and the lack of a procedure to audit data collectors' work. In some cases, results from post-cycle and post-round surveys for the same campaigns have been substantially different. Adjustments to methodology will be needed for the context of coverage surveys for LLINs and for working in a different geography. As of March 2021, we are in discussions with Malaria Consortium about the design of monitoring for these campaigns and are considering (a) adding additional types of monitoring and evaluation to help triangulate results and (b) playing a more active role in designing data quality cont

rows.label: Total adjustment for quality of monitoring and evaluation
Change of priorities
rows.explainer: Funding will be tied to a specific, very time-limited use. After discussions with Malaria Consortium, we expect that Malaria Consortium will return unused funds or allow GiveWell to redirect unused funds to another Malaria Consortium program—most likely SMC, which is similarly cost-effective, according to our models.

rows.label: Non-funding bottlenecks
rows.explainer: Funding will be tied to a specific, very time-limited use. After discussions with Malaria Consortium, we expect that Malaria Consortium will return unused funds or allow GiveWell to redirect unused funds to another Malaria Consortium program—most likely SMC, which is similarly cost-effective, according to our models.

rows.label: Within-org fungibility
rows.explainer: Our understanding is that it is extremely unlikely that, in the absence of GiveWell-directed funding, Malaria Consortium would have funded some or all of these funding gaps either with unrestricted funding or restricted funding that it could have directed to other Malaria Consortium programs. Malaria Consortium has limited unrestricted funding relative to the size of this program. We think it's unlikely that Malaria Consortium would have dedicated fundraising efforts to this program otherwise. We learned of this funding gap because GiveWell specifically funded Malaria Consortium to identify funding gaps for LLIN campaigns in countries it has a presence in.

How much does it cost the government to increase ln(income) by one unit through education?
rows.explainer:
For comparison, the median GiveWell estimate of cost per unit increase in ln(consumption) for GiveDirectly was $394 (as of November 2017).

We guess that government spending on primary education is roughly as valuable as giving to GiveDirectly, secondary education is roughly 70% as valuable as GiveDirectly, tertiary education is roughly 50% as valuable as giving to GiveDirectly. 

We take weighted averages of these guesses based on actual government expenditure in Uganda.

For more details see: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/15_gs-zfPDRnFHs4uWDOJGzo1pccntqIA4XAK5aa4OBA/edit#gid=0)

How much does it cost the government to increase ln(income) by one unit through social security?
rows.explainer:
For comparison, the median GiveWell estimate of cost per unit increase in ln(consumption) for GiveDirectly was $394 (as of November 2017).

We guess that government spending on in-kind social security and social pensions is roughly 70% as valuable as GiveDirectly, and conditional and unconditional cash transfers are roughly as valuable as GiveDirectly. 

We take weighted averages of these guesses based on actual government expenditure in Uganda.

For more details see: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/15_gs-zfPDRnFHs4uWDOJGzo1pccntqIA4XAK5aa4OBA/edit#gid=0)

rows.explainer: The last LLIN campaign in Anambra was in 2014, so as of 2021, the subsequent campaign was four years overdue. Since government entities didn't fund a campaign in 2017-2021, it's unlikely that they will do so in 2021-2023, the period when LLINs from a GiveWell-funded campaign will be in place. More generally, we haven't encountered examples of domestic governments funding LLIN campaigns. It is possible that this campaign, and any leftover LLINs that are given to clinics, will crowd out some funding from the government of Anambra for LLINs delivered through "routine" channels (e.g. at antenatal or vaccination visits to clinics).
